The length of the millennium need not be exactly 1,000 years; what matters is an intermediate earthly reign between the Parousia and the eternal state.

Papias of Hierapolis (as reported by Irenaeus and Eusebius), Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 80-81, appealing to Revelation and Isaiah 65), Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.32-36, who saw the kingdom as creation's restoration), Tertullian, Hippolytus and Lactantius taught a future earthly reign of Christ after his return. Justin admitted other orthodox Christians disagreed.

Origen's allegorical exegesis, Dionysius of Alexandria's doubts about Revelation, Eusebius's disparagement of Papias, reaction against crudely materialistic chiliasm, and above all Augustine's City of God made amillennialism dominant. The Reformers, reacting to radical Anabaptist millenarianism (e.g. Münster, 1534-35), also rejected chiliasm.

Joseph Mede's Clavis Apocalyptica (1627) and Johann Heinrich Alsted revived premillennialism among learned Protestants, typically within a historicist reading of Revelation. In the 19th century Henry Alford's Greek Testament (with his famous argument on Revelation 20:4-5), Horatius Bonar and C. H. Spurgeon held premillennial views independent of Darby's dispensationalism.

George Eldon Ladd of Fuller Seminary gave the view its modern scholarly form, critiquing pretribulationism in The Blessed Hope (1956) and developing inaugurated eschatology in The Presence of the Future (1974). Robert Gundry's The Church and the Tribulation (1973) and Douglas Moo's contribution to the 1984 rapture debate defended posttribulationism.

Craig Blomberg and Sung Wook Chung's A Case for Historic Premillennialism (2009), Wayne Grudem's Systematic Theology, and many Reformed Baptist and broadly evangelical scholars hold the view, offering it as an alternative to both dispensationalism and amillennialism.
Takes the sequence of Revelation 19-20 and the parallel use of 'came to life' in Revelation 20:4-5 at face value.
Has the earliest documented support among post-apostolic writers (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus).
Avoids the Israel-church dichotomy and the recent pretribulational scheme while still affirming a future earthly reign.
Explains Old Testament prophecies of an earthly age in which death still occurs but life is prolonged (Isaiah 65:20) better than views that place their fulfilment only in the eternal state.
Integrates well with inaugurated eschatology: the kingdom is present now but its public, earthly vindication awaits Christ's return.

Only one passage (Revelation 20) explicitly teaches an intermediate kingdom, while many clearer texts join the resurrection of righteous and wicked and the final judgment in a single event (John 5:28-29; Acts 24:15; 2 Thessalonians 1:6-10).

Historic premillennialists reply that progressive revelation often gives later detail to earlier outlines, and that one clear text is sufficient. They also find hints of an interval elsewhere: 1 Corinthians 15:23-24 lists Christ, then those who are his at his coming, then 'the end' (eita), and Old Testament texts such as Isaiah 24:21-23 speak of punishment 'after many days'.
It is implausible that resurrected, glorified saints would coexist with mortal people on an earth where sin and death still exist.

The risen Jesus lived and ate among mortal disciples for forty days (Acts 1:3; Luke 24:41-43). Premillennialists regard the mixed state as a purposeful transition from the present age to the eternal state.
A final rebellion after a thousand years of Christ's visible rule seems incoherent and undermines the completeness of his victory at his return.

Premillennialists see it as a final demonstration of the depth of human sin, which rebels even under ideal conditions and with Satan restrained, and of the justice of God's final judgment. Revelation 20:7-10 explicitly places such a rebellion after the thousand years.
Dispensationalists object that historic premillennialism blurs Israel and the church and leaves the literal land and kingdom promises to Israel unfulfilled.

Historic premillennialists follow the New Testament's application of Israel's promises to the one people in Christ (Galatians 3:29; Ephesians 2:11-22) while still affirming, with Romans 11, a future salvation of ethnic Israel; the millennium on a renewed earth also gives the land promises a real, earthly fulfilment.
The early chiliasm it claims as ancestor was materialistic (Papias's vines of 10,000 branches), and the Fathers themselves largely abandoned it.

Modern proponents do not adopt the extravagant details, but argue that Irenaeus's central conviction, that God will redeem and restore his physical creation, is thoroughly biblical, and that the early chiliasts' antiquity counts in the view's favour even if their particulars do not bind.
Patristic chiliasm

The view of Papias, Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian and Lactantius: after Antichrist's reign Christ returns, raises the righteous and reigns from a rebuilt Jerusalem for a thousand years in an earth of abundance. Some tied it to a 'world week' of six thousand years followed by a sabbath millennium. It was a hope of creation restored rather than a dispensational scheme.
Posttribulational premillennialism (mainstream)

The dominant modern form (Ladd, Gundry, Moo, Blomberg, Grudem): the church endures the great tribulation and is gathered at Christ's single, visible return. The Greek apantēsis ('to meet', 1 Thessalonians 4:17) is read as the welcome party that goes out to escort a visiting king back to the city, so the saints rise to meet the Lord and return with him to earth.
Covenantal premillennialism

Held by some Reformed and Particular Baptist theologians and Presbyterian premillennialists (historically including Horatius Bonar), who combine covenant theology's one people of God, often a future conversion of Israel, and a premillennial reading of Revelation 20, without dispensational distinctives.
Historicist premillennialism

From Joseph Mede (1627) through Isaac Newton and E. B. Elliott's Horae Apocalypticae (1844), many premillennialists read Revelation as a sequential outline of church history, often identifying the papacy with Antichrist and calculating the 1,260 days as years, with the millennium following Christ's return. It is uncommon today.
Dispensational Premillennialism
Disp. Premil
God keeps his promises to Israel: rapture, tribulation, then a literal thousand-year reign.

Dispensationalists describe their approach as “consistent literal” or “normal” (grammatical-historical) interpretation applied to prophecy as to the rest of Scripture. They speak of God's distinct programmes for Israel and the church, of the church as a “mystery” revealed in the New Testament, of the “blessed hope” (Titus 2:13) of an imminent pretribulational rapture, and of a literal millennial kingdom in which God keeps his unconditional covenants with national Israel.

Dispensational premillennialism holds that God's unconditional covenants with Abraham, David and Israel (the land, the throne, the new covenant) will be fulfilled literally to the nation of Israel in a future thousand-year reign of Christ from Jerusalem. The church, begun at Pentecost, is a distinct people; in most forms it will be raptured before a seven-year tribulation that fulfils Daniel's seventieth week (Daniel 9:24-27), during which Antichrist rises and Israel is refined and turns to its Messiah. Christ then returns visibly, judges the nations and reigns for a literal millennium, after which Satan's final rebellion, the great white throne judgment and the eternal state follow. The system has classic, revised and progressive forms, and its adherents differ on rapture timing.
A consistent literal (normal, grammatical-historical) hermeneutic, applied to prophecy as well as to history, so that promises made to Israel are fulfilled to Israel.

A distinction between Israel and the church: the church, which began at Pentecost (Acts 2; 1 Corinthians 12:13), was a 'mystery' not revealed in the Old Testament (Ephesians 3:3-6) and does not replace or absorb national Israel (Romans 11:1, 29).
God's ultimate purpose in history is his own glory, displayed through several programmes, not solely through redemption (Ryrie's 'doxological' principle).
Daniel's seventy weeks (Daniel 9:24-27) contain a gap between the 69th and 70th weeks; the 70th week is a future seven-year tribulation in which Antichrist makes and breaks a covenant with Israel.

In most forms, the rapture of the church is pretribulational and imminent (John 14:1-3; 1 Thessalonians 1:10; 4:13-18; 5:9; Revelation 3:10), distinct from Christ's later return to earth with his saints.
After the tribulation Christ returns, Israel as a nation repents and is saved (Zechariah 12:10; Romans 11:26), and the nations are judged (Matthew 25:31-46).

Christ then reigns on David's throne from Jerusalem for a literal thousand years, fulfilling the Abrahamic, Davidic and new covenants to Israel (2 Samuel 7:12-16; Jeremiah 31:31-37; Ezekiel 36-37; 40-48), with Satan bound.
Salvation in every age is by grace through faith in God, though the content of revelation and stewardship (dispensation) differs.

Dispensationalists see the early chiliasts as forebears of premillennialism (not of pretribulationism), note Protestant schemes of 'dispensations' (e.g. Pierre Poiret, Isaac Watts), and point to occasional earlier hints of a pre-tribulation removal of saints, such as the Baptist Morgan Edwards (1788) and a disputed sermon attributed to Pseudo-Ephraem; the significance of these precursors is disputed.

John Nelson Darby and the Plymouth Brethren, especially through the Powerscourt prophecy conferences (1831-33), systematised the Israel-church distinction, the 'parenthesis' church age and the pretribulational rapture. The claim that the rapture idea originated in Margaret MacDonald's 1830 vision or Edward Irving's circle is disputed; dispensationalists such as Thomas Ice deny it.

The view spread in America through the Niagara Bible Conferences (1876-97), D. L. Moody's circle, and above all the Scofield Reference Bible (1909; 1917). Lewis Sperry Chafer founded Dallas Theological Seminary (1924) and wrote an eight-volume dispensational systematic theology.

Charles Ryrie's Dispensationalism Today (1965), John Walvoord's The Millennial Kingdom (1959) and J. Dwight Pentecost's Things to Come (1958) refined the system, softening the 'two peoples forever' language. Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970) and later the Left Behind novels (1995-2007) made it hugely popular.

From the Dispensational Study Group (1986) and Craig Blaising's 'Developing Dispensationalism' articles (1988), Blaising, Darrell Bock and Robert Saucy developed progressive dispensationalism. Revised dispensationalism remains strong (Thomas Ice, The Master's Seminary), and Michael Vlach has restated the case against supersessionism.
Treats God's unconditional promises to Abraham, David and Israel as irrevocable (Romans 11:29) and takes national Israel's future seriously.
Offers a coherent, consistently applied hermeneutic that reads prophecy in its plain sense, as many fulfilled messianic prophecies were fulfilled literally.
Takes the sequence of Revelation 19-20 and the details of Daniel and the Olivet Discourse as describing concrete future events.
Stresses imminence and the 'blessed hope', motivating holiness, evangelism and watchfulness (Titus 2:11-14; 1 John 3:2-3).
Progressive dispensationalism has integrated inaugurated eschatology and the unity of God's kingdom programme while keeping Israel's distinct future, opening dialogue with other traditions.
The pretribulational rapture is absent from the first eighteen centuries of church history and appears only in the 1830s.

Dispensationalists answer that the test of a doctrine is Scripture, not antiquity, and that doctrinal clarification often comes late (as with justification at the Reformation). They also point to possible precursors (Morgan Edwards, 1788; a Pseudo-Ephraem sermon, whose interpretation is disputed) and to the early church's belief in imminence.
Inserting a gap of nearly two thousand years between the 69th and 70th weeks of Daniel 9 is arbitrary.

Dispensationalists point to other prophetic gaps, such as Jesus stopping mid-sentence when reading Isaiah 61:1-2 (Luke 4:18-20), and note that Daniel 9:26 places the Messiah's 'cutting off' and the city's destruction after the 69th week without placing them in the 70th, which implies an interval.
The New Testament applies Israel's titles and promises to the church (Galatians 3:29; 6:16; 1 Peter 2:9-10; Acts 15:14-18), which undermines a strict Israel-church distinction.

They read 'the Israel of God' (Galatians 6:16) as Jewish believers, and argue that the church shares in Israel's blessings (Ephesians 2:12-13) without inheriting Israel's national, territorial promises. Progressive dispensationalists frame this as inclusion of the Gentiles alongside a restored Israel, not replacement (Romans 11:29).
The 'consistent literal' hermeneutic is applied inconsistently, since dispensationalists also recognise symbols (beasts, horns, a woman clothed with the sun).

'Literal' means the normal sense intended by the author, including figures of speech; dispensationalists hold that symbols in prophecy have concrete, identifiable referents (real persons, nations, events) rather than being dissolved into timeless principles.
Classic dispensationalism appeared to teach two ways of salvation (law and grace), and the popular movement has been marked by date-setting and speculative headline exegesis.

Dispensational scholars (Ryrie, Walvoord, Blaising and Bock) affirm one way of salvation by grace through faith in every age, differing only in the content of revelation; ambiguous wording in the original Scofield notes was revised in the New Scofield Reference Bible (1967). Scholarly dispensationalists disavow date-setting (Matthew 24:36).

Darby, Scofield and Chafer (c. 1830-1950): God has two peoples with two destinies, a heavenly people (the church) and an earthly people (Israel), whose distinction continues into eternity. The church age is a 'parenthesis' unforeseen by the prophets; the kingdom offered by Jesus was postponed when Israel rejected it. Usually seven dispensations are distinguished (innocence, conscience, human government, promise, law, grace, kingdom).

Ryrie, Walvoord, Pentecost and later Thomas Ice (c. 1950-present): drops the eternal heavenly/earthly dualism, so all the redeemed share the eternal state, but keeps the Israel-church distinction in God's historical programmes, the postponed Davidic kingdom, and Ryrie's 'sine qua non': a consistent literal hermeneutic, the Israel-church distinction, and the glory of God as history's unifying purpose.

Blaising, Bock and Saucy (1986-present): Jesus already sits on David's throne at the Father's right hand since the ascension (Acts 2:30-36), so the Davidic kingdom is inaugurated now and consummated in the millennium. The church is not a parenthesis but a phase of the one kingdom plan, in which Jews and Gentiles share new covenant blessings, while national Israel retains a distinct, future territorial and political restoration. It uses a 'complementary' hermeneutic, allowing New Testament expansions of Old Testament promises without cancelling their original sense. Traditional dispensationalists such as Ice regard it as a significant departure.
Pretribulational rapture

The majority dispensational view (Walvoord, Pentecost, Ryrie, Ice): Christ comes for his church before the seven-year tribulation, removing it from the period of God's wrath (1 Thessalonians 1:10; 5:9; Revelation 3:10). Arguments include imminence (no prophesied event must precede the rapture), the absence of the word 'church' in Revelation 4-19, the need for mortal believers to populate the millennium, and the distinct purposes of the tribulation for Israel. The rapture (Christ comes for his saints, in the air) is distinguished from the Second Coming (Christ comes with his saints, to the earth).
Midtribulational rapture

Defended by Gleason Archer in the 1984 three-views volume: the church is raptured at the midpoint of the seventieth week, before the 'great tribulation' of the final three and a half years (Daniel 9:27; Matthew 24:15-21). It often links the 'last trumpet' (1 Corinthians 15:52) with the seventh trumpet (Revelation 11:15) and the ascension of the two witnesses (Revelation 11:11-12). It holds that God's wrath falls only in the second half. It has few current advocates.
Prewrath rapture

Developed by Robert Van Kampen and Marvin Rosenthal (The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church, 1990) and today by Alan Kurschner: the church will face Antichrist's persecution in the second half of the seventieth week, but that 'great tribulation' is cut short (Matthew 24:22) by the cosmic signs of the sixth seal (Revelation 6:12-17; Matthew 24:29-31), at which Christ raptures his people before the Day of the Lord's wrath (the trumpet and bowl judgments). Wrath is God's, tribulation is man's and Satan's. It is futurist and premillennial, but many proponents do not hold dispensational distinctives.
Posttribulational rapture

The rapture and the visible Second Coming are one event after the tribulation (Matthew 24:29-31; 2 Thessalonians 2:1-8). The church is preserved through, not removed from, the tribulation (John 17:15; Revelation 3:10 read as protection). This is chiefly the historic premillennial view (Ladd, Gundry, Moo, Blomberg), though some futurists with dispensational sympathies hold it; Gundry's The Church and the Tribulation is its standard defence.
Spiritual Understanding
Spiritual
Revelation is the unveiling of Jesus Christ and his finished work, read as present spiritual reality, not a forecast to fear.

Proponents describe their approach simply as reading Revelation for what its first verse says it is: 'the revelation of Jesus Christ' (Revelation 1:1), an unveiling of a Person rather than a timetable of disasters. The Lamb standing 'as though slain' at the centre of the throne (Revelation 5:6) is, for them, the key that opens every seal: the cross is the centre of history and the lens for every symbol. They speak of reading 'from victory, not toward fear', of the 'finished work' ('It is finished', John 19:30; 'It is done', Revelation 16:17 and Revelation 21:6), of union with Christ, the renewal of the mind and the new creation. The book, they say, shows the old order (law as a way of life, the flesh, self-effort, religious systems of mixture) giving way to the new (grace, the Spirit, rest), and invites every reader to see Christ and live from him now.

The Spiritual Understanding is a Christ-centred symbolic reading of Revelation. It shares idealism's conviction that the visions portray timeless realities and preterism's attention to the book's first-century setting, but it makes two moves of its own. First, every vision is read Christologically: each chapter is expected to unveil something of the person of Jesus and what he accomplished at the cross. Second, the symbols are applied chiefly to present spiritual experience: union with Christ, the believer's identity, the renewal of the mind, and the contest between the old (flesh, law, fear, a religion of self-effort) and the new (Spirit, grace, rest). The book is organised around paired opposites: two cities (Babylon and the New Jerusalem), two women (the harlot and the Bride), two marks (the beast's mark and the Father's name on the forehead), the beasts against the Lamb, and, implicitly, two trees (the tree of the knowledge of good and evil set against the tree of life in Revelation 22). Typical keys include the forehead as the mind and the hand as one's works, 666 as the number of humanity striving short of God's sabbath rest, the 144,000 as the complete people of God, and the thousand years as the fullness of Christ's present reign. Judgments are read as falling on the old order, sin, death and the accuser rather than on believers. Most proponents affirm a final appearing of Christ and the consummation of all things, though they place the weight of the book on what is already true in Christ. It overlaps strongly with amillennial and postmillennial 'present reign' readings and differs most sharply from futurist readings that place most of the book in a future tribulation.
Revelation is 'the revelation of Jesus Christ' (Revelation 1:1): its purpose is to unveil a Person, so every chapter should be read for what it shows of Christ and the cross.
The Lamb 'as though slain' (Revelation 5:6) is the key to the book: the Lion conquers as a Lamb, and the cross is the decisive victory from which all the visions are read.

The symbols speak mainly of spiritual realities that are true now: union with Christ, the believer's identity and seal, the renewal of the mind, and the passing of the old order before the new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The finished work governs the judgments: they fall on sin, death, the accuser and the old system of law and self-effort, so believers read the book from victory and not toward fear (John 19:30; Revelation 12:10-11; Revelation 21:6).

The book is built on paired opposites: Babylon and the New Jerusalem, the harlot and the Bride, the beast's mark and the Father's name, the beasts and the Lamb, the tree of knowledge and the tree of life.

The forehead stands for the mind and the hand for one's doing: the 'mark of the beast' is a mind and life shaped by the flesh, fear and self-effort, while the seal of God is the Spirit and the Father's name, a new identity (Revelation 7:3; Revelation 14:1; Ephesians 1:13).
The thousand years symbolise the fullness of Christ's present reign, and the 'first resurrection' is the new birth into union with the risen Christ (Revelation 20:4-6; Ephesians 2:5-6).

The New Jerusalem 'coming down out of heaven' is the Bride, the people of God in union with Christ: grace from above rather than a tower built from below, with the tree of life (Christ himself) at its centre (Revelation 21:2; Revelation 22:1-2).

Clement of Alexandria and especially Origen read Scripture as having a 'spiritual' sense beneath the letter, and treated the Apocalypse's images (the New Jerusalem, the thousand years) as pictures of the soul's union with the Word rather than an earthly kingdom. Origen's rejection of literal chiliasm in On First Principles set a precedent that this view still appeals to.

The North African Tyconius read Revelation as a portrait of the church's present life, a body of two parts in which Christ and the devil each have their 'city'. Augustine took up this reading in City of God (Book XX): the first resurrection is the soul's rising through faith, and the thousand years are Christ's present reign in the church. The 'two cities' theme is central to the Spiritual Understanding.

Commentators such as Bede, and the wider tradition of the 'four senses' of Scripture (literal, allegorical, moral and anagogical), read the Apocalypse for what it teaches about Christ, the soul's life and the heavenly goal. Proponents see their own 'present reality' readings as a recovery of the moral and allegorical senses, anchored in Christ.

Luther's test for Scripture was whether it 'promotes Christ', and the Reformers stressed justification as a gift and union with Christ. Puritans such as John Owen and Thomas Goodwin made communion with Christ central, and Owen read the 'shaking of the heavens' (Hebrews 12:26-28) as the passing of the old covenant order. Proponents draw on these emphases, although the Reformers and Puritans themselves mostly read Revelation historically.

William Milligan's lectures (1886) and William Hendriksen's More Than Conquerors (1940) popularised Lamb-centred symbolic readings. Since the late twentieth century, grace-centred churches and chapter-by-chapter teaching series have combined this symbolic heritage with an emphasis on the finished work, identity in Christ, the renewal of the mind and the believer's present share in the new creation. This has produced the distinctive 'Spiritual Understanding' of Revelation as an unveiling of Christ rather than a forecast of catastrophe.

Takes the book's own title seriously: Revelation 1:1 announces a revelation 'of Jesus Christ', and the slain-yet-standing Lamb really is the book's central image (Revelation 5:6), named some 28 times.

Pastorally freeing: it removes fear-driven speculation and date-setting and directs readers to worship, assurance and faithful living, as the book's own beatitudes do (Revelation 1:3; Revelation 22:7).
Recognises the book's genre: apocalyptic symbols (numbers, beasts, cities, women) are signs (Revelation 1:1, 'signified') to be interpreted, not literal snapshots.

Integrates Revelation with the rest of the New Testament, where union with Christ, new creation, the seal of the Spirit and the defeat of the accuser are present realities (2 Corinthians 5:17; Ephesians 1:13; Colossians 2:15).

The 'two cities, two women, two marks' structure illuminates real literary contrasts in the book, which many scholars also recognise (e.g. Babylon as harlot versus the New Jerusalem as Bride in Revelation 17–22).

It risks allegorising: by applying symbols mainly to inner experience (the forehead as the mind, the sea as the unrenewed soul), it can detach the book from its concrete setting of persecuted first-century churches facing Rome and the imperial cult, and from what John's first readers would have understood.

Proponents answer that they affirm the historical setting and read it as the first layer: Babylon was Rome (and Jerusalem's apostate system) for the first readers. But the symbols were chosen from the Old Testament to carry timeless meaning, and the New Testament itself applies such images spiritually (Galatians 4:24-26 on the two Jerusalems; Hebrews 12:22). Controlling the symbols by Christ and by Scripture's own usage, they argue, guards against arbitrary allegory.

Some keys (for example forehead = mind, 666 = human effort short of 7, sea = the restless mind) are not stated in the text and can seem imposed. Different teachers may assign different meanings, which makes the method hard to test.

Proponents point to biblical precedent for each key: the forehead and hand in Deuteronomy 6:8 (the law bound to mind and deed), the sea as restless and wicked humanity in Isaiah 57:20 and Revelation 17:15, six as humanity's day short of the seventh-day rest (Genesis 2:2; Hebrews 4:9-10). They grant that application varies, but argue that every reading must exalt Christ and fit the whole of Scripture.

By concentrating on present spiritual realities, it can underplay the book's future hope: the visible return of Christ, the bodily resurrection, the final judgment and the renewal of the physical creation (Revelation 1:7; Revelation 20:11-15; Revelation 21:1-5).

Most proponents explicitly affirm Christ's appearing and the consummation; they object only to making fear of a future tribulation the book's centre. The 'already' of union with Christ, they argue, is the guarantee of the 'not yet' (Colossians 3:1-4), and reading the end through the finished work is what the book intends.

The emphasis on judgment falling on 'the old order' and on the believer reading 'from victory' may soften the book's real warnings to churches (Revelation 2–3), its calls to endurance under suffering, and its sober depiction of judgment on the unrepentant (Revelation 14:9-11; Revelation 20:15).

Proponents reply that the warnings are real but are addressed to believers as calls to return to their 'first love' and to the grace already given (Revelation 2:4-5), not threats designed to produce fear. They treat the lake of fire as the end of all that opposes life, while acknowledging that its scope and nature are interpreted differently within the view, and they hold that endurance is the fruit of seeing the Lamb's victory (Revelation 12:11).
Finished-work reading

Centres everything on the cross as the completed victory: 'It is finished' (John 19:30) and 'It is done' (Revelation 16:17; Revelation 21:6). The seals, trumpets and bowls are read as the outworking of that victory against sin, death, the accuser and the old covenant system.
Union and identity reading

Applies the symbols mainly to the believer's inner life: the seal and the Father's name on the forehead as a renewed mind and identity in Christ, the mark of the beast as a mindset of flesh and fear, the seven churches as conditions of the heart, and the first resurrection as the new birth.
Covenantal-spiritual (preterist-leaning) reading

Combines Christ-centred symbolism with a first-century anchor: Babylon includes apostate Jerusalem and its temple system, AD 70 marks the end of the old covenant age (Hebrews 8:13), and the New Jerusalem is the new covenant people of God, while the symbols remain timeless for believers today.

The most common pairing among contemporary postmillennialists. The Olivet Discourse's tribulation and much of Revelation (usually dated before AD 70, a date that is disputed) are read as fulfilled in Jerusalem's fall, clearing the stage for the gospel's worldwide advance; Revelation 20 describes the present age, which ends with Christ's future bodily return.

Full preterists typically regard the millennium as the transitional 'last days' of roughly AD 30–70, ending with Christ's coming in AD 70. Formally this places the Parousia after the millennium, so some full preterists describe their view as postmillennial in structure and expect the kingdom to keep growing indefinitely; but because they deny any future bodily return, resurrection and final judgment, historic postmillennialists (who are creedal) reject the pairing. Some full preterists came out of postmillennial-preterist circles.

Historically the classic pairing: Puritans, Jonathan Edwards (following Moses Lowman's scheme) and many 19th-century Protestants read Revelation as an outline of church history, with the papacy as Antichrist and the fall of 'Babylon' and the conversion of the Jews ushering in the latter-day glory. Common in the 17th–19th centuries; uncommon among postmillennialists today, who mostly favour preterism.
